title: The Guest Daksha Left Out
hookLine: Daksha holds a great sacrifice and leaves out his son-in-law Shiva; Sati goes anyway
carry: the ash Daksha mocked, Shiva's devotees wear
tomorrow: can the god of love make Shiva fall in love?

cards: From Kailash, Sati sees them go by in the sky: gods and their wives, dressed for a celebration, heading to her father's house. Daksha, her father, is holding a great sacrifice, a yajna, and the guests are streaming in.
Everyone, it seems, except Sati and her husband. Daksha has left out his own son-in-law, Shiva. Sati turns to her husband and says she wants to go.
A family quarrel that shakes the world.

teach.h: AN OLD GRUDGE AT A GATHERING.
teach.b: The grudge is old. At an earlier gathering of the gods, Daksha walked in and the others rose to honor him, but Shiva stayed seated. Daksha never forgave it.
To him, Shiva was an embarrassment: smeared with ash, wandering cremation grounds.
Shiva warns Sati not to go uninvited, but surely her own family won't turn her away. She goes, and it's worse than he said.

teach.h: A PERFECT RITUAL, AND NO SHIVA.
teach.b: There's no portion set aside for Shiva at all. Her father greets her coldly and scorns her husband before everyone.

Sati rebukes her father before the gods, and then, the story says, she gives up her body by the power of her own yoga, rather than live as the daughter of the man who mocked Shiva. Shiva's grief becomes fury.
From his matted hair he brings out Virabhadra, a terrible warrior, who wrecks the sacrifice. Daksha is killed.

teach.h: A GOAT'S HEAD AND A SECOND CHANCE.
teach.b: When the gods beg, Shiva relents, and Daksha lives again with a goat's head: a proud man, humbled. Now the teaching. Daksha's ritual was flawless.

What he left out was the Lord. Many teachers read Daksha as pride itself, the ego that can sit right inside religion, getting every detail right and shutting God out. And look at what he mocked: the ash.
To this day Shiva's devotees wear sacred ash, vibhuti, often as three lines across the forehead. Many say it's a reminder: the body ends in ash, and only God remains.
Read with Daksha, pride ends in ash too. So today, when you catch yourself looking down on someone, or getting every detail right while leaving God out, remember the ash.
If this story stirs thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

how: Hindus tell the story of Sati and Daksha's sacrifice in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas; Shaiva temples honor Virabhadra, Sati's story is linked to the shakti pithas, places sacred to the goddess, and Shiva's devotees wear sacred ash, vibhuti, often as three lines on the forehead.

games.q: you're Sati. your father is holding a great sacrifice and has invited the gods but not your husband. your husband says don't go. what does Sati do in the story?
o: go to your father's house anyway.
send a messenger to ask why.
games.why: Sati goes, sure her family won't turn her away. it's worse than Shiva said, and she will not hear him mocked.

practice: Many Shiva devotees start the day by drawing sacred ash across the forehead in three lines, saying Om Namah Shivaya. Try the gesture now, with or without ash.

Let one bit of pride come to mind, a grudge you polish or someone you look down on, and for one breath let it be ash. If you pray, say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use. If you don't, simply say: this too goes to ash.
